source.title: Not All Data Are Unlearned Equally
source.authors: Aravind Krishnan; Siva Reddy; Marius Mosbach

record.tranche_reason: The study reports that unlearning efficacy depends on training frequency and that low generation scores can coexist with retained information in biography completion or probabilistic evaluations, qualifying claims of uniform successful removal.
record.gate_note: The experiments evaluate unlearning and alternative ways of eliciting or measuring target knowledge, but do not perform the proposed fine-tuning, activation-ablation, quantization, jailbreak, or language-switch attacks. Paraphrased questions are part of the evaluation; the study does not compare paraphrased prompts against an otherwise matched prompt condition as a recovery attack. Figures report many results without numerical values in the text; those rows are marked figure_only.
record.test_reason: Its own results show target QA suppressed while biography completion or few-shot True/False probability still carries the target fact, mainly for high-frequency data and larger models. That bears on A (removal) and on C's 'access blocked rather than deleted'. No fine-tuning, ablation, quantization or jailbreak attack is run.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Authors conclude frequent pretraining data is harder to unlearn, across methods and scales. They find generation- and probability-based evaluations of forgetting and utility disagree, and the disagreement grows with model size. They call for frequency-aware methods and more comprehensive, generation-weighted evaluation.
record.recipe_differences: Uses Gradient Ascent, SIMNPO, and refusal training with additional question-token regularization; does not reproduce the cited unlearning recipes or test the specific recovery attacks in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Unlearning outcomes vary with data frequency, model size, unlearning method, dataset, and evaluation type. The authors also report sensitivity of OLMo Gradient Ascent and SIMNPO to hyperparameter configurations.
record.problems: Most plotted outcomes are not numerically reported in the text. The study uses co-occurrence counts as a proxy for frequency, and its OLMo unlearning was sensitive to hyperparameters. It does not test the proposed recovery attacks directly.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant result rows omitted.

untested.parts: Robustness to simple recovery attacks; near-chance against a stated chance baseline.
Activation-direction ablation; any causal internal edit.
No controlled rephrasing, jailbreak, language or in-context attack. BIO-completion and True/False prompts are evaluation formats, not attacks versus a matched control.
All: no robust counter-method proposed or tested.

missing.what: Per-dataset OLMo refusal-training results (generative vs probabilistic, high vs low count), including the books exception
GPT-2 SIMNPO and refusal utility (QA Utility panels)

record.verdict_notes: Reader version codes V1/V3 remapped to A/C. BIO-retention and True/False-retention rows are linked to C; they also imply knowledge is not removed (against A), but they are not double-linked because rows carry one state. These elicitation formats could arguably bear on E, but there is no matched attack design. All values are figure-only; Rouge-L, not chance-referenced. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No systematic test of the listed recovery attacks. The study does not establish near-chance performance against a stated chance baseline.
No fine-tuning on unrelated, loosely related, or subset relearning examples to recover knowledge.
No activation-direction ablation. Persistence is assessed through biography completion and probabilistic evaluation, not a causal internal edit.

No controlled test of prompt rephrasing as a recovery attack, jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context recovery. Paraphrased questions are used for evaluation, without a matched prompt-form comparison.
No newer method is tested for resistance to the listed recovery attacks.

relation.reason: Its own results on QA vs BIO and True/False probability bear on versions A and C.

tranche.reason: The study argues that apparent unlearning on generative QA can hide retained knowledge (BIO, True/False), depending on frequency and scale. That calls for restating A and bears on C. T3 is a plausible alternative.

source_check.notes: All values are figure-only except the stated numbers (below 20%, 25%, 10%, +20%, 98%, 0.99, 99%). OLMo target evals are normalized to initial values; three seeds; no chance level. No recovery attacks (fine-tuning, ablation, quantization, prompting) were run; the retain set doubles as the regularization set.

statements.correction: To add if wanted: OLMo-7B-0724-SFT, SIMNPO, capitals: low-count targets are forgotten faster and further than high-count on paraphrased generative eval (Fig 6, figure only). The text says the trend holds across datasets and methods.
statements.problem: Cites r12 and r13 but describes no result from this study. None of its numbers (0.766, 0.918, LLaMA, Qwen, TOFU) are from this study. Nothing it says about the study is wrong.

statements.correction: Refusal (IDK) training, GPT-2 20M-210M: target BIO never below 98%, either split (Fig 8). GA (Fig 5) and SIMNPO (Fig 7): high-count keeps more BIO than low-count (+20%, GPT-20M, employer, GA) while QA falls below 20%; the QA/BIO divergence widens with size. OLMo-7B SFT (capitals, books, ZSRE): where high-count paraphrased performance drops, True/False performance stays >=99% of initial.
statements.problem: The BIO-persists/widening-gap clause is from GA and SIMNPO, but it names no method and follows 'refusal training'. The text states >=99% only where high-count paraphrased performance drops. The conditions line omits OLMo's real-world facts.

statements.correction: GPT-20M, GA, employer: with target QA below 20%, high-count keeps +20% more target BIO than low-count. Across sizes (GA, SIMNPO), high-count is unlearned less effectively. OLMo-7B SFT (real capitals, books, ZSRE): low-count generative and True/False performance falls lower than high-count.
statements.problem: Minor: the 20-point gap is GA, employer attribute, GPT-20M (text writes '+20%'). The conditions line 'synthetic or from-scratch settings' does not fit the OLMo-7B part, which uses real-world facts on a pretrained model.
